items: Science is not just a set of facts — it is a process: a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown. We learn it by doing activities and experiments, every answer opens new questions, and it comes with responsibility for our planet.
Science is a process — a way of thinking, not just a list of facts.
It welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown.
Grade 7 asks deeper questions: How do things work? Why do events happen the way they do? What can we learn from patterns in nature?
We learn science by stepping out of the book and classroom — activities and experiments are stepping stones.

The Grade 7 journey begins with materials around us: their properties (sour fruits, haldi stains), the properties that make a lamp glow (metals and non-metals), the changes they go through (some reversible, some not), how heat flows, and how the Sun's heat moves water.
Materials have properties we can explore: why are some fruits sour? what happens when we wash a haldi stain?
Testing which materials make a lamp glow helps us classify materials — metals and non-metals.
Changes happen all around us; some can be reversed and others cannot (an ordinary torch battery that runs out can't be used again).
Some changes happen, or happen faster, when things are heated; heat flows (ice cube, glacier).

notes.h: Life, Time, Light and the Sky
items: Not only materials change — our bodies change too. The journey goes from life processes in animals and plants, through the question 'what is time?', to clocks and shadows, to light, and finally to the shadows of the Earth and Moon that give eclipses — and to day and night.
Not only materials — our bodies change too, especially in the middle-school years.
Life processes — eating, breathing, blood carrying nutrients — are essential for all animals to survive.
Plants also need food to grow; the book asks how they get it and whether they breathe.
Over time, life on Earth has evolved to do all this in a beautiful, carefully balanced way.

notes.h: Thinking Like a Scientist: Asking Questions
items: Every chapter asks you to observe, experiment and think carefully. To think like a scientist, asking interesting questions matters as much as finding answers — Activity 1.1 turns things around: given an answer, invent curious questions that could lead to it.
The chapters invite you to make observations, do experiments and think carefully — each builds on what you already know.
Great scientists don't just answer questions — they ask amazing ones.
'To be a wise person, you must be a whys person.'
There are never any wrong questions — let your imagination run wild, but ask interesting, not obvious ones.
Wrong: Science is just a set of facts to learn from a textbook. Right: Science is a process — a way of thinking that welcomes curiosity, asks questions and is open to the unknown
Wrong: Every change can be undone. Right: Some changes can be reversed and others cannot — an ordinary (non-rechargeable) torch battery that runs out can't be used again
Wrong: Eating and breathing matter only for humans. Right: Life processes are essential to all animals, and plants also need food to grow
Wrong: Science is only about finding answers to the questions we are given. Right: To think like a scientist, asking interesting questions is equally important

items: Substances around us are acidic, basic or neutral. Litmus sorts them into three groups; acidic things taste sour, basic things taste bitter and feel slippery, neutral things are neither.
Three natures: acidic, basic, neutral
Acidic: blue litmus → red; sour
Basic: red litmus → blue; bitter and slippery
Neutral: no change in either litmus
Litmus, obtained from lichens, shows one colour in acids and another in bases, so it is an acid-base indicator; indicators can be natural or synthetic.
Litmus comes from lichens
Indicator = different colours in acid and base

items: An extract of red rose petals turns red in acidic and green in basic solutions, so it is a natural acid-base indicator; many flowers and vegetables work the same way.
Prepare: fallen petals → wash → crush → hot water → wait → filter
Red in acid, green in base, no change in neutral
Many coloured flowers and vegetables are natural indicators
Turmeric paper turns red in basic substances but stays yellow in acidic and neutral ones, so it tests bases only.
Turmeric paper: yellow → red in base
No change in acid and neutral
Use litmus or rose extract to tell acid from neutral

Olfactory = sense of smell

Useful when colour cannot be seen
When an acid and a base are mixed in sufficient quantity they cancel each other's effect: salt and water form and heat is given out.
Acid + Base → Salt + Water + Heat
Needs sufficient quantity
Excess of either side changes the nature again
Many everyday problems — an ant bite, soil that is too acidic or basic, acidic factory waste — are managed by neutralising them with the opposite kind of substance.
Treat with the opposite nature
Ant bite: acid ← baking soda
Acidic soil ← lime; basic soil ← organic matter

notes.h: Electric Lamp: Incandescent Lamp and LED
items: An incandescent lamp glows because its thin filament gets hot; an LED has no filament and has a positive (longer) and a negative (shorter) wire.
Filament gets hot and glows

items: A lamp glows only when its two terminals are joined to the two different terminals of a cell, making a complete path for current; current is taken to flow from + to −, and an LED lets it pass one way only.
Lamp glows only with a complete path
Current: + to − (outside the cell — added)

items: A switch is a simple device that completes (ON, closed circuit) or breaks (OFF, open circuit) a circuit; it can be placed anywhere in the circuit.
Switch ON = closed circuit = current flows
Switch OFF = open circuit = air gap, no current
A switch can be placed anywhere in a circuit

Each electrical component has a symbol; a circuit drawn with these symbols is its circuit diagram — easy to draw and understand everywhere in the world.
Circuit diagram = circuit drawn with symbols
Long line +, short line −
LED triangle points the way current flows

Materials through which current flows easily are conductors (metals); those through which it cannot pass are insulators (plastic, rubber, ceramics …). Both are needed: conductors carry current, insulators protect us.
Conductors: current flows easily — metals (and pencil lead)
Insulators: current cannot pass — plastic, rubber, ceramics, wood, glass
Copper for wires
Body conducts — handle electricity with dry hands

items: Copper, aluminium and iron are lustrous (metallic lustre) and hard — they are metals; coal, sulfur and wood are non-lustrous and not as hard. Some metals break the rule: sodium and potassium are soft, mercury is a liquid.
Metals: lustrous (metallic lustre) and generally hard.
Coal, sulfur, wood: non-lustrous, not as hard.
Exceptions: sodium, potassium soft; mercury liquid.

Malleability is the property by which materials can be beaten into thin sheets. Most metals are malleable (gold and silver the most); coal and sulfur are brittle; wood is neither malleable nor brittle.
Malleable = can be beaten into thin sheets (most metals).
Brittle = breaks into pieces (coal, sulfur).
Gold and silver are the most malleable.
Ductility is the property by which materials can be drawn into wires; it is mainly possessed by metals. Coal and sulfur are not ductile.
Ductile = can be drawn into wires (mainly metals).
1 g gold → 2 km wire.
Coal and sulfur are not ductile.
Sonority is the property of metals that enables them to produce a ringing sound; metals are sonorous. Coal and wood give dull sounds.
Sonorous = gives a ringing sound when struck.
Metals are sonorous; coal and wood are not.
Bells, ghungroos use sonority.

Transfer of heat from one point to another of a material is conduction; materials that transfer heat are conductors. Metals are good conductors of heat, wood is a poor conductor — so vessels are metal and handles are wood.
Conduction = heat moves from point to point in a material.
Metals: good conductors of heat; wood: poor.
Metal vessels, wooden/plastic handles.

Materials that let electricity flow through them easily are good conductors; those that do not are poor conductors. In the tester only metals make the bulb glow, so metals are good conductors of electricity.
Good conductors let electricity flow — metals.
Poor conductors stop it — plastic, rubber, wood, sulfur, coal.
Metals are generally hard, lustrous, malleable, ductile and good conductors of heat and electricity.

Iron gets a brown deposit called rust only when both air and water (moist air) are present; this is rusting. Gradual deterioration of metal surfaces by air, water or other substances is corrosion. Rusting can be prevented by painting, oiling, greasing or galvanisation.
Rust needs air + water (moist air).
Rusting is the corrosion of iron.
Prevent: paint, oil, grease, galvanise (zinc).

notes.h: Metals with Oxygen and Water: Basic Oxides
items: Magnesium burns in air with a dazzling white flame and forms white magnesium oxide; its solution turns red litmus blue, so it is basic. Oxides of metals are generally basic. Some metals like sodium react vigorously with oxygen and water.
Magnesium + Oxygen → Magnesium oxide.
Metal oxides are basic — red litmus turns blue.
Sodium kept in kerosene (reacts vigorously with air and water).

Sulfur burns in air to form sulfur dioxide, which dissolves in water to give sulfurous acid — acidic. Sulfur does not react with water. Substances like sulfur and phosphorus are non-metals: usually soft and dull, not malleable, ductile or sonorous, poor conductors, with acidic oxides. Non-metal + oxygen → acidic oxide (SO₂ → sulfurous acid).
Non-metals: dull, soft, brittle, not sonorous, poor conductors.
Sulfur does not react with water; phosphorus kept under water.
Metals and non-metals are elements; plastic, wood, glass are not.

Properties decide uses.
Non-metals are essential: O, C, N, Cl, I.
Alloys, special metals, recycling.

Are all metals hard and solid?: No. Sodium is soft and mercury is a liquid

notes.h: Ignition Temperature and the Fire Triangle

notes.h: Changes That Can and Cannot Be Reversed
items: Some changes can be reversed — we get the original object or substance back (melting ice can be refrozen); others cannot (chopped vegetables, popcorn).
Ask: can I get the SAME object or substance back?
Being reversible or not is a different question from physical or chemical

The situation decides: decay is bad in the store, good in the compost pit

notes.h: Slow Natural Changes: Weathering and Erosion

Erosion by wind and water is a physical change

items: Like a seedling, a human must grow and mature before it can reproduce. Adolescence is the stage between childhood and adulthood (about 10 to 19 years) when this happens.
Up to about 10–12 years most changes are in height and weight; after that other changes begin — adolescence.
Each person goes through the stages at their own pace; durations differ.
Changes are physical, emotional and behavioural; some are seen, some happen inside.

notes.h: Physical Changes, Secondary Sexual Characteristics and Puberty
items: In adolescence the body grows taller and stronger, the voice changes, hair appears and pimples may come. Changes that tell males from females but are not used in reproduction are secondary sexual characteristics; they mark the onset of puberty.
Timing, nature and extent of changes vary between individuals — completely normal.
Secondary sexual characteristics mark the onset of puberty.
Inside the body, parts involved in reproduction mature. In girls the menstrual cycle begins; its bleeding phase, menstruation, is natural and a sign of good reproductive health.
Menstruation is natural and a sign of good reproductive health.
Its end at 45–55 marks the end of reproductive capability in a woman's life.
Adolescence brings stronger emotions than childhood — mood swings, sensitivity — which change behaviour; understanding them helps us make better choices.
Adolescence is marked by stronger emotions than childhood.
Understanding how emotions influence behaviour helps us make better choices and respond thoughtfully.
Most changes of adolescence — menstruation and other signs of puberty — are mainly due to hormones, chemicals made in our body and released at the right time on signals from the brain.
Hormones regulate growth and development for proper functioning of the body.
Some hormones influence mood and behaviour.

notes.h: Nutrition and Physical Activity in Adolescence
items: A growing adolescent body needs a nutritious diet — proteins, carbohydrates, fats, vitamins and minerals such as calcium and iron — and regular physical activity.
For proper growth we need proteins and carbohydrates, and also enough fats, vitamins and minerals.
Calcium → bones; proteins → growth, strength, energy; iron → blood.

Menstrual hygiene is essential for comfort and health.

items: Heat moves from the hotter part of an object to the colder part; each heated particle passes heat to its neighbour, but the particles themselves stay in place. In solids heat moves mainly by conduction.

In solids heat is transferred mainly by conduction.

notes.h: Good and Poor Conductors of Heat
items: Materials that let heat pass easily (metals) are good conductors; materials that do not (wood, glass, clay, porcelain, air) are poor conductors or insulators. Trapped air, a poor conductor, keeps us and our houses warm or cool.
Metals → good conductors → cooking utensils.
Wood, glass, clay, porcelain and air → poor conductors (insulators).
Trapped air is used in clothes, blankets and walls.
In liquids and gases the heated part expands, becomes lighter and rises, while the cooler, heavier part comes down to take its place; heat is carried by the actual movement of particles.
Warm air or water expands, becomes lighter and rises.
Cooler, heavier air or water comes down to take its place.
In liquids and gases heat is transferred by convection.

Land heats up and cools down faster than water. By day warm air over land rises and cooler air moves from the sea to the land (sea breeze); at night the land is cooler, so cooler air moves from land to sea (land breeze).
Land heats and cools faster than water.
Day → sea breeze (sea to land); night → land breeze (land to sea).
Land and sea breezes are examples of convection.
In radiation heat travels directly from a hot object to us without needing any medium; the Sun's heat reaches the Earth this way, and all objects radiate heat.
Conduction and convection need a medium; radiation does not.

Convection: particles actually move.

The water cycle redistributes and replenishes water in rivers, lakes and oceans.
It conserves the total amount of water on the Earth.

Surface water seeps through soil and rocks (infiltration) — fastest where the spaces between particles are wide, open and connected — and is stored as groundwater in aquifers, which we reach with wells. Groundwater is not unlimited, so it must be recharged and conserved.
Groundwater is not unlimited: growing population pulls out too much, while less vegetation and more concrete reduce infiltration.
The water cycle recharges groundwater.

notes.h: What a Plant Needs to Grow
items: As a plant grows, new leaves and branches appear, it gets taller and its stem thickens. A fair test with three pots shows that a plant needs both sunlight and water to grow.
Change only ONE thing between pots (a fair test)
Plants need both sunlight and water to grow

notes.h: Starch in Leaves — the Iodine Test
items: Plants store food as starch, made in their broad, flat leaves. The iodine test shows starch: a decolourised leaf turns blue-black with iodine.

items.text: Decolourising removes the green colour so the colour change (and so the starch) is easy to see

items: Blue-black = starch present; no change = no starch

notes.h: Chlorophyll and Sunlight — Leaves as Food Factories
items: Starch is made only in the green parts of a leaf and only when the plant gets sunlight. Chlorophyll is essential to make starch in sunlight, so leaves are the 'food factories' of plants.
Green + sunlight → starch
Chlorophyll is essential for making starch
Leaves = food factories

notes.h: Role of Air — Carbon Dioxide and the Name Photosynthesis
items: A leaf part kept away from carbon dioxide makes no starch, so carbon dioxide from the air is essential. Making food from carbon dioxide and water in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll is called photosynthesis.
Four needs: sunlight, water, chlorophyll, carbon dioxide

items.text: A leaf is the primary site of photosynthesis; other green parts with chlorophyll also photosynthesise
Animals get their food from plants, directly or by eating animals that eat plants

items: Plants do not only take in substances — during photosynthesis they release oxygen. A water plant in sunlight gives off bubbles of a gas that makes a lit matchstick burn with an intense flame.
Oxygen supports burning — a lit matchstick flares up
No sunlight → no photosynthesis → no oxygen bubbles

Photosynthesis uses carbon dioxide and water, in the presence of sunlight and chlorophyll, to make glucose and release oxygen; glucose gives instant energy and is later converted into starch for storage.
IN: carbon dioxide + water
ON THE ARROW: sunlight + chlorophyll
OUT: glucose + oxygen
Glucose → starch for storage
A thin peel from the lower surface of a leaf shows tiny pores called stomata; through them the leaf exchanges carbon dioxide and oxygen.
Carbon dioxide enters and oxygen leaves through stomata during photosynthesis
Stomata also exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide during respiration (book summary)

notes.h: Transport in Plants — Xylem and Phloem
items: Water and minerals taken up by the roots move up to all parts through thin tubes called xylem; food made in the leaves moves to all parts through another set of tubes called phloem, and may be stored in seeds and roots.
Xylem: water + minerals, from roots upward
Phloem: food, from leaves to all parts
Plants respire: they break down glucose using oxygen, releasing carbon dioxide, water and energy for growth, in all parts. Photosynthesis and respiration together keep the gases balanced.

items.text: All parts of a plant, green or non-green, carry out respiration

items: Plants have ways to make, move and use food to get energy

items.text: Bottle garden: a sealed plant keeps growing because CO₂ from respiration is used in photosynthesis and O₂ from photosynthesis in respiration

items: Wrong: Plants eat food from the soil through their roots, like animals eat. Right: Roots take up water and minerals; plants do not eat food — the next videos show they make it
Wrong: The alcohol step is to kill germs on the leaf. Right: It removes the green chlorophyll so the blue-black colour can be seen
Wrong: The whole leaf makes starch, whatever its colour. Right: Only the green patches (with enough chlorophyll) turned blue-black
Wrong: Plants take in oxygen from the air to make food. Right: It is carbon dioxide from the air that is used to make food
Wrong: The bubbles are just air trapped in the water. Right: They appear only in sunlight and make a matchstick burn brightly — they are oxygen from photosynthesis
Wrong: Starch is made directly in photosynthesis. Right: Glucose is made first; it is later converted into starch for storage

sol_items: If all photosynthesising organisms disappeared: There would be no food or oxygen, so all life would end
A potato slice shows starch with iodine: where does thi...: Food is made in leaves and sent by phloem; the potato stores it as starch
Does the broad flat shape of leaves help photosynt: Yes, a large surface takes in more sunlight and carbon dioxide
X + Y → carbon dioxide + Z + energy: X = glucose, Y = oxygen, Z = water
Two potted plants, one in sunlight and one in the : It tests the need for sunlight; the dark plant turns pale and grows weak
Vani's four set-ups: Starch forms only with sunlight and carbon dioxide, and oxygen is given out only there
imp_items: What is photosynthesis?
Making food by plants from carbon dioxide and water using sunlight
Write the equation of photosynthesis in words.
Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen (in sunlight)
Name the green pigment in leaves.
Chlorophyll
How do we test for starch?
With iodine, which turns it blue-black
What are the raw materials of photosynthesis?
Carbon dioxide, water and sunlight
Why do leaves become pale in the dark?
Without light the plant cannot make chlorophyll and food

notes.h: Sources of Light: Luminous and Non-luminous Objects
items: Objects that emit their own light are luminous (Sun, stars, lightning, fire, fireflies, electric lamps); objects that do not are non-luminous — the Moon only reflects the Sun's light.
Luminous = emits its own light
Non-luminous = does not emit light; seen only when light falls on it
The Sun is the main natural source; electric lamps are the main artificial sources today

notes.h: Light Travels in a Straight Line
items: Light travels in a straight line: we get a spot of light or see a flame only when the holes or the pipe are in one straight line.
Light travels in a straight line
Holes must be in one line, a pipe must be straight, for light to pass
This one idea explains shadows and the pinhole camera
When an object is placed in the path of light, light passes almost completely through transparent materials, partially through translucent materials, and not at all through opaque materials.
Transparent — almost all light passes
Translucent — some light passes
Opaque — no light passes
Predict first, then observe and compare

Because light travels in a straight line, an opaque object in its path blocks it and leaves a dark patch — the shadow. A shadow needs a light source, an opaque object and a screen; its shape, size and sharpness depend on where the object is between the source and the screen.
Shadow = dark patch where light is blocked
Needs: light source + opaque object + screen
Closer to the torch → bigger shadow; closer to the screen → smaller and sharper (sharper: added)
The shadow lies on the side away from the light
A mirror or shiny surface changes the direction of light falling on it — this is reflection of light. Light still travels in straight lines before and after it falls on the mirror.
Reflection = change in direction of light by a mirror
Light travels straight before and after reflection
Tilting the mirror moves the reflected spot

The thing placed in front of a mirror is the object; what appears behind the mirror is its image. A plane-mirror image is the same size as the object, erect, cannot be obtained on a screen, and is laterally inverted; it appears near when the object is near and far when it is far.
Object in front, image behind the mirror
Same size, erect, not on a screen, laterally inverted
Image near when object is near

In a pinhole camera, light from an object passes through a tiny hole and forms an image on a screen. Because light travels in straight lines, the image is upside down (inverted), and it shows the colours of the object.
Light through a tiny hole forms an image on a screen
The image is inverted and coloured
Straight-line travel makes the rays cross at the hole

Mirrors can be combined to make useful items: a periscope uses reflection from two plane mirrors to see objects not directly visible; a kaleidoscope uses three mirrors whose reflections of reflections make ever-changing patterns.
Periscope — 2 mirrors in a Z-shaped box — see what is not directly visible
Kaleidoscope — 3 mirrors in a triangle — reflections of reflections make patterns
Both work by reflection of light
Wrong: The Moon makes its own light because it shines at night. Right: The Moon is non-luminous — it reflects sunlight that falls on it
Wrong: Light can follow a bent pipe the way water flows through it. Right: The flame disappears when the pipe is bent — light goes straight and hits the pipe wall
Wrong: Translucent is just another word for transparent. Right: Translucent lets only part of the light through — the spot becomes dim
Wrong: A red object casts a red shadow. Right: Changing the colour of an opaque object does not change the colour of its shadow — it stays dark
Wrong: A mirror makes its own light — that is why we see a bright spot. Right: The mirror only changes the direction of sunlight or torch light falling on it
Wrong: The image becomes smaller when the object moves away from the mirror. Right: The image is always the same size as the object; it only looks smaller because it appears farther away

sol_items: Which are luminous: Mars, Moon, Pole Star, Sun, Venus, ...: Pole Star and Sun; the rest only reflect light
Measure your shadow at 9 AM, 12 PM and 4 PM: when is it...: At 12 noon, when the Sun is highest
Statements: image in a plane mirror is laterally invert...: Both are true; T and O are symmetrical about the vertical line
Can a bent tube with two plane mirrors make a peri: Yes; place one mirror at each bend, tilted at 45°, facing each other
Why is a high-flying bird's shadow not seen but a low o...: A high shadow spreads out and is too faint; a low one is dark and sharp
Sketch the image in a pinhole camera: The image is inverted and formed on the screen opposite the hole
imp_items: What is a luminous object?
An object that emits its own light, such as the Sun
Give two non-luminous objects.
Moon and a book
How does light travel?
In a straight line
Explain the formation of a shadow with an activity.
Hold an object between a torch and a screen and observe the dark patch
Differentiate transparent, translucent and opaque.
Transparent lets most light pass, translucent some, opaque none
How is a shadow formed?
When an opaque object blocks light

The Earth spins on its own axis, which passes through the North and South Poles, once in about 24 hours, from West to East
Day and Night
Sunlight falls on only the half of the Earth that faces the Sun

items: The Earth spins on its own axis, which passes through the North and South Poles, once in about 24 hours, from West to East. Because we watch from this turning Earth, the Sun only appears to move across the sky.
One rotation takes about 24 hours
Direction: West → East (anticlockwise seen from above the North Pole)
The Sun appears to move because we watch it from a turning Earth
Sunlight falls on only the half of the Earth that faces the Sun. As the Earth rotates from West to East, every place turns into the light (sunrise) and out of it (sunset), so day and night repeat.
Half of the Earth is always lit
Rotation West → East brings each place into light and darkness
Eastern places see sunrise first

notes.h: Apparent Motion of the Sun, Moon and Stars
items: Because the Earth rotates from West to East, the Sun, the Moon and the stars all appear to rise in the East, cross the sky and set in the West. The Pole Star, very close to where the axis points, stays almost still and the other stars seem to circle it.
Everything in the sky appears to move East → West
The Pole Star appears nearly still
Stars seem to circle the Pole Star

notes.h: Revolution of the Earth and the Changing Night Sky
items: While rotating, the Earth also revolves around the Sun in a nearly circular orbit, once in about 365 days and 6 hours. As it moves, its night side faces different directions in space, so the stars seen after sunset change through the year.
Revolution = around the Sun, about 365 days 6 hours
Orbit nearly circular
Same date and time → same stars every year

The Earth's axis is tilted and keeps the same tilt as the Earth goes round the Sun. Because the Earth is round, the hemisphere tilted towards the Sun gets more intense sunlight for more hours — summer — while the other hemisphere has winter.
Seasons = tilted axis + round Earth
Summer = more intense sunlight + longer days
Hemispheres have opposite seasons
Distance from the Sun is NOT the reason

notes.h: Solstices, Equinoxes, the Equator and the Poles
items: In the Northern Hemisphere the longest day is around 21 June (summer solstice) and the shortest around 22 December (winter solstice); around 21 March and 23 September daytime is 12 hours (equinoxes). The Equator always has 12-hour days, while the poles get six months of sunshine and six months of darkness.
Summer solstice ~21 June, winter solstice ~22 December
Equinoxes ~21 March and ~23 September: 12-hour day
Equator: always 12 h; poles: 6 months day, 6 months night

A solar eclipse happens when the Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth and blocks sunlight. The small Moon can cover the huge Sun because it is much closer, so their apparent sizes are similar. The Sun must never be looked at directly, even during an eclipse.
Solar eclipse: Sun – Moon – Earth
Total solar eclipse lasts only a few minutes because the Earth rotates and the Moon moves, so the shadow moves
Never view the Sun directly

A lunar eclipse happens when the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon and blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon; the Earth's shadow falls on the full Moon. A totally eclipsed Moon looks dark red, and it is safe to watch with the naked eye.
Lunar eclipse: Sun – Earth – Moon
Total lunar eclipse: Moon looks dark red
Safe to watch with naked eyes
Wrong: The Sun really travels across the sky from East to West every day. Right: The Sun only appears to move; it is the Earth that turns
Wrong: Day and night happen because the Earth goes around the Sun. Right: They happen because the Earth rotates on its axis; one trip around the Sun takes a whole year
Wrong: Stars stay fixed all night; only the Sun and the Moon move across the sky. Right: Stars also rise in the East and set in the West; the Big Dipper turns around the Pole Star
Wrong: Rotation and revolution are the same motion. Right: Rotation is spinning on its own axis (about a day); revolution is going around the Sun (about a year)

Wrong: When the Northern Hemisphere tilts towards the Sun it has summer because it is closer to the Sun. Right: The change in distance is very small; summer comes from more intense sunlight for more hours
Wrong: Every place has 12 hours of day and 12 hours of night every day. Right: Only the Equator always does; elsewhere day length changes and is 12 hours only on the equinoxes

sol_items: A lunar eclipse occurs when the Sun comes between the E...: False; the Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
Sunrise happens earlier in Gujarat than in Jharkha: False; Jharkhand is east, so it sees sunrise first
The Earth's revolution causes day and night: False; rotation does
Orion was overhead at 8 pm yesterday: About 4 minutes earlier, at about 7:56 pm
Daytime in India, night in the USA: The Earth is a sphere and only the half facing the Sun has day
Why can the small Moon block the Sun completely?: The Moon is much closer, so it looks about the same size as the Sun
imp_items: What is rotation?
The spinning of the Earth on its axis
Why do we have day and night?
Only the half of the Earth facing the Sun has day
In which direction does the Earth rotate?
West to East
What is revolution?
The Earth moving around the Sun in a year
Why do seasons occur?
Because of the tilt of the Earth's axis and revolution
When is the summer solstice in the Northern Hemisphere?
Around 21 June
